questions.q: What does a canary deployment actually do with live traffic?
options: It routes all traffic to the new version immediately, then rolls back if there's a problem
It routes a small percentage of real traffic to the new version, then gradually increases that percentage if the version looks healthy
It duplicates every request and sends identical copies to both versions forever
It only sends traffic to the new version during scheduled maintenance windows
questions.explain: Canary starts at a small percentage — commonly around 10% — and steps the weight up (10% → 25% → 50% → 100%) with a pause at each step to watch how the new version behaves.

questions.q: What distinguishes a blue-green deployment from a canary deployment?
options: Blue-green has no rollback path at all once the switch happens
Blue-green only applies to database migrations, never to application code
Blue-green gradually increases traffic the same way canary does, just under a different name
Blue-green runs two full, independent environments and switches all traffic from one to the other instantly, rather than shifting a percentage gradually
questions.explain: Blue (current live version) and green (new version) are both complete environments; once green is verified, traffic is switched all at once, typically by repointing a load balancer or a Service selector.

questions.q: What is the main advantage of canary's gradual traffic shift, in terms of blast radius?
options: If the new version has a bug, it only ever affects a small percentage of users before the rollout can be caught and halted
It eliminates the need for any monitoring during the rollout
It guarantees the new version has zero bugs before reaching 100%
It removes the need for a rollback mechanism entirely
questions.explain: Canary's core advantage is a small blast radius — a problem surfaces at 10% of traffic, not 100%, giving a chance to halt the rollout before most users are affected.

questions.q: What is the main cost of a blue-green cutover compared to a canary rollout?
options: Blue-green requires the new version to be tested in production first, which canary does not
Blue-green cannot be automated and must always be done manually
The cutover is all-or-nothing — the instant you switch, 100% of traffic hits the new version at once, so any undetected bug affects every user immediately
Blue-green always costs less than canary because it only needs one environment
questions.explain: Because the switch happens in one move rather than gradually, there's no small-percentage buffer to catch a problem before it reaches all users — plus running two full environments typically costs more during the overlap.

questions.q: In the Argo Rollouts canary step `- setWeight: 25` followed by `- pause: { duration: 5m }`, what is happening?
options: The Rollout controller sends 25% of traffic to the new ReplicaSet and holds that weight for 5 minutes before considering whether to advance
The rollout waits 25 minutes before sending any traffic at all
25% of the pods are deleted and replaced every 5 minutes indefinitely
The new version receives no traffic until the full 5-minute pause completes
questions.explain: setWeight sets the percentage of traffic routed to the new ReplicaSet, and pause holds that weight for the given duration before the controller moves to the next step — exactly what the YAML in this lesson defines.
